texts.title: City bets on night buses to save its late-night economy
q: Why did the council extend the night bus service?
To support workers and businesses that operate late at night.
What does the trial cost each year?
About £2.4 million.
What worries the opposition councillors?
That the money could be spent on daytime routes used by more people.
paras: The city council has announced that night bus services will run seven days a week from next spring, in a move it hopes will breathe new life into a late-night economy that has struggled since the pandemic.

Until now, only four routes operated after midnight, and only on Fridays and Saturdays. Under the new plan, twelve routes will run every thirty minutes between midnight and five in the morning, linking the city centre with the main hospitals, the airport and the largest residential districts.

Council leader Maria Okafor said the decision was about fairness as much as nightlife. "We often talk about the night-time economy as if it were just bars and clubs," she said. "But it is also cleaners, nurses, security guards and kitchen staff. Many of them have been paying for expensive taxis or walking home alone in the dark. That simply isn't acceptable."

The two-year trial will cost around £2.4 million a year, funded partly by a small increase in parking charges in the city centre. Business groups have welcomed the plan. A spokesperson for the local hospitality association said that several restaurants had cut their opening hours because staff could not get home.

However, not everyone is convinced. Opposition councillors argue that the money would be better spent on improving daytime routes, which carry far more passengers. "Of course night workers deserve support," said councillor Tom Reeve, "but we have daytime buses that are packed and late every single morning. We need to get the basics right first."
The council says it will publish passenger figures every three months and will review the scheme if demand turns out to be lower than expected.

texts.title: Supermarkets quietly shrink products as shoppers tighten their belts
q: What is "shrinkflation"?
Reducing the size or quantity of a product while keeping the price the same.
Which products were most affected, according to the consumer group?
Snacks, breakfast cereals and household cleaning products.
What change does the consumer group want?
Clear labels on shelves when a product's size has been reduced.
paras: Shoppers who suspect that their favourite chocolate bar has been getting smaller are not imagining it. A report published this week by a leading consumer group found that more than a third of the products it monitored had been reduced in size over the past two years, while their prices either stayed the same or, in some cases, actually went up.

The practice, widely known as "shrinkflation", is not illegal, provided the new weight or volume is printed on the packaging. Critics argue, however, that it is deliberately misleading, since few customers check the small print on a familiar product before putting it in their trolley.

The report singled out snacks, breakfast cereals and household cleaning products as the worst offenders. One well-known brand of washing-up liquid had shrunk from 500ml to 433ml, a reduction of more than 13 per cent, with no change to the design of the bottle.

Manufacturers insist that they have been left with little choice. Energy, packaging and transport costs have risen sharply, and companies say that customers are more resistant to a visible price rise than to a slightly smaller pack. "Consumers consistently tell us that the price on the shelf is what matters most," said a spokesperson for the food and drink industry, adding that firms were "working hard to absorb costs wherever possible".

The consumer group is now calling on the government to require supermarkets to display a clear notice on the shelf whenever a product's size has been cut, for at least six months after the change. Several European countries have already introduced similar rules, and early evidence suggests that the practice has become noticeably less common as a result.

For now, the group's advice is simple: compare the unit price, the cost per 100 grams or per litre, rather than the headline price. It is a small habit, but over a year it can add up to a surprising amount.

texts.title: The quiet unravelling of a once-celebrated housing policy
q: What was the original aim of the policy?
To help first-time buyers onto the property ladder by subsidising deposits.
According to economists, what was the main unintended effect?
It pushed up house prices, so much of the subsidy ended up with developers and sellers.
Why is it difficult for the government to abandon the scheme?
Because it is popular with voters and the construction industry has come to depend on it.
paras: When the scheme was unveiled a decade ago, it was hailed as a rare piece of policy that would please almost everyone. Young people priced out of the housing market would receive a generous top-up to their deposits; builders would enjoy a steady stream of buyers; and the government could claim to be restoring the dream of home ownership to a generation that had all but given up on it.

Ten years and several billion pounds later, that consensus has quietly unravelled. A cross-party committee this week concluded that the scheme had, in all likelihood, done more to inflate prices than to widen access. Its report, couched in the measured language such documents favour, nonetheless amounts to a damning verdict: a substantial share of the subsidy, it found, had been "capitalised into prices", which is to say that it ended up in the pockets of developers and sellers rather than buyers.

None of this would have surprised economists, many of whom warned at the outset that subsidising demand in a market where supply is notoriously sluggish was bound to push prices up. What is striking is how long it took for those warnings to be heeded. Part of the explanation lies in the politics. Schemes that hand money to identifiable voters are easy to defend and hard to withdraw, and the construction industry, having grown accustomed to state-backed demand, lobbied hard for each successive extension.

Ministers now find themselves in a difficult position. Scrapping the scheme outright risks a sharp slowdown in house building at precisely the moment the country needs more homes, not fewer. Yet extending it again would be difficult to reconcile with the committee's findings. The likeliest outcome, insiders suggest, is a gradual winding down, dressed up as a "reform" and accompanied by promises to tackle the supply side through planning changes.

Whether those promises amount to anything more than rhetoric remains to be seen. Successive governments have pledged to overhaul the planning system, and successive governments have retreated in the face of local opposition. The lesson of the past decade, the committee notes, is that "there is no shortcut around the need to build".

texts.title: Flatmates: the washing-up war
paras: MAYA: Okay, we need to talk about the kitchen.
LEO: Is this about the pan? I was going to wash it. I'm literally about to do it.
MAYA: Leo, it's been there since Tuesday. It's got its own ecosystem now.
LEO: That's a bit harsh. It's just soaking.
MAYA: For four days? It's not soaking, it's living there. Look, I don't want to nag you, I really don't. But I'm sick of coming home and having to clear up before I can even make a cup of tea.
LEO: Fair enough. I've been snowed under with work, that's all. I keep meaning to sort it out.
MAYA: I get that, honestly. We're all busy. So how about a schedule? We take turns, one week each, and whoever's on duty does the bins as well.
LEO: A schedule. Like at school.
MAYA: Like adults who share a kitchen. And if you can't do your week, you just swap with someone. No drama.
LEO: Okay, okay. You've got a point. But can I make one tiny suggestion?
MAYA: Go on.
LEO: Can we get a dishwasher? They're not that expensive second-hand, and it'd save us all a lot of arguments.
MAYA: Who's going to pay for it?
LEO: We split it three ways. Sam won't mind, he hates washing up more than I do.
MAYA: That's not saying much. Fine, look into it. But until it turns up, the schedule starts tomorrow. And you're first.
LEO: Why am I first?
MAYA: Because the pan is still in the sink.
LEO: ...Right. Point taken.

texts.title: The interview that went off-script
paras: INTERVIEWER: So, Daniel, thanks for coming in. Let's start with the obvious question. Why do you want to leave your current job?
DANIEL: Honestly? I've outgrown it. I've been there four years, and I've taken on more and more, but the role hasn't really kept pace with that. I'm ready for something more challenging.
INTERVIEWER: That's a very polished answer. Now give me the real one.
DANIEL: (laughs) Wow, okay. You don't beat around the bush, do you?
INTERVIEWER: Not if I can help it. We've got forty minutes, and I'd rather spend them finding out who you actually are.

DANIEL: Fair enough. The real answer is that my manager takes credit for everything. Last quarter I came up with a plan that cut our delivery times by a third, and by the time it reached the board it had somehow become his idea.
INTERVIEWER: And how did you handle that?

DANIEL: Badly, at first. I got moody, if I'm being honest. Then I realised that sulking wasn't getting me anywhere, so I started copying the board into my progress updates. Politely. Just so the paper trail spoke for itself.
INTERVIEWER: Did it work?
DANIEL: Up to a point. People upstairs know who did the work now. But it's made things a bit frosty between us, and I don't want to spend the next five years walking on eggshells.
INTERVIEWER: That's a far more interesting answer than the first one.
DANIEL: Is it a better one, though?
INTERVIEWER: It's an honest one, which is rarer than you'd think. Let me ask you something else. If you joined us and found yourself in the same situation, what would you do differently?

DANIEL: I'd raise it early, face to face, before it festered. I let it slide for far too long, assuming it would sort itself out. It didn't, and by then it had turned into a much bigger deal than it needed to be.
INTERVIEWER: Good. Right, let's talk about the role itself.

texts.title: Dinner with the in-laws
paras: RUTH: More wine, Patrick? Or are you still pretending you only drink on special occasions?
PATRICK: I'm told this counts as one. It isn't every day your daughter brings home a man who's read the whole of Proust.
JAMES: Read is a generous word. I skimmed a fair amount of it, if I'm honest.
PATRICK: Ah, an honest man. That's even rarer. Tell me, James, what is it you do, exactly? Clare was rather vague on the phone.
CLARE: I wasn't vague, Dad. I said he works in policy.
PATRICK: Which covers a multitude of sins.
JAMES: It does, to be fair. I advise a charity on housing, mostly. Which basically means writing reports that ministers thank us for and then quietly ignore.
RUTH: Well, that sounds thoroughly depressing.

JAMES: It has its moments. Every so often something we've been banging on about for years turns up in a speech as if somebody had just thought of it. You learn to take your victories where you can find them.
PATRICK: A realist. I suppose that's preferable to an idealist. They tend to be exhausting company.
CLARE: Dad was an idealist until about 1983.
PATRICK: I was a young man, and it was a different country. Besides, idealism is a luxury of people who have never had to balance a budget.

JAMES: With respect, I'd say it's the other way round. The people balancing the budgets are the ones who most need to remember what the money is for. Otherwise you end up with spreadsheets that add up and policies that don't.
RUTH: (after a pause) Well. I think he'll do, Patrick.
PATRICK: Hmm. Ask me again after the cheese course.

texts.title: The return of the urban beekeeper
q: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN: Urban honey is usually lower in quality than rural honey.
FALSE (urban bees often have a wider variety of plants, so the honey can be better).
TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN: Paris has more beehives than London.
NOT GIVEN
Complete: Some ecologists worry that too many hives compete with wild ______ for food.
pollinators
Which measure does the text say is more useful than adding hives?
Planting more flowers and reducing pesticide use.
paras: Over the past twenty years, beekeeping has moved from the countryside to the rooftops. Hotels, offices and even opera houses in cities such as London, Paris and New York now keep hives, and the number of amateur urban beekeepers has risen sharply.

At first glance, cities might seem an unlikely place for bees. Yet urban environments can be surprisingly rich in food. Parks, private gardens, railway embankments and street trees provide a variety of flowering plants throughout the year, whereas much modern farmland is planted with a single crop that flowers for only a few weeks. As a result, honey produced in cities often contains pollen from a wider range of plants, and some beekeepers argue that its flavour is more complex as a result.

The popularity of urban beekeeping is partly a response to widely reported declines in bee populations. Many people see keeping a hive as a practical way of helping the environment. However, a growing number of ecologists have raised concerns about this assumption. Honeybees are just one of hundreds of species of bee, most of which are wild and solitary. In areas where hives are densely concentrated, honeybees may compete with these wild pollinators for limited supplies of nectar and pollen.

Researchers in one European capital found that as the number of hives in the city increased, the amount of food available per bee fell considerably. They concluded that adding more hives was unlikely to benefit wild bees and might even harm them.

For this reason, many conservation groups now encourage people who want to help bees to focus on habitat instead. Planting a wider variety of flowers, leaving some areas of grass uncut and reducing the use of pesticides are, they argue, far more effective than installing another hive.

texts.title: Why we procrastinate
q: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN: According to the passage, procrastination is mainly caused by poor time management.
FALSE (researchers see it as a problem of managing emotions).
Complete: People tend to put off tasks that make them feel anxious, bored or ______.
insecure / resentful (either)
What is meant by "temporal discounting"?
Valuing immediate rewards more than future ones.
Which strategy involves imagining your future self?
Increasing the sense of connection with one's future self so that the long-term consequences feel real.
paras: For decades, procrastination was treated as a failure of organisation. The standard advice was to make lists, set deadlines and break large tasks into smaller ones. While such techniques can certainly help, a growing body of psychological research suggests that they address the symptoms rather than the cause. Procrastination, many researchers now argue, is fundamentally a problem of managing emotions rather than time.

According to this view, people do not delay tasks because they are lazy or unaware of the deadline. Rather, they avoid tasks that trigger unpleasant feelings, such as anxiety, boredom, self-doubt or resentment. Putting the task off brings immediate relief, which in turn reinforces the habit. The next time a similar task appears, the brain has learnt that avoidance works, at least in the short term.

A second factor is what economists call "temporal discounting": the tendency to value rewards that are available now more highly than rewards in the future. The satisfaction of finishing an essay lies weeks away; the pleasure of watching another episode of a series is immediate. Neuroimaging studies have even suggested that, when people think about their future selves, the pattern of brain activity resembles that seen when they think about strangers.

These findings have led to new approaches to tackling the problem. One is to practise self-compassion. Surprisingly, students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next, perhaps because they no longer associated studying with guilt. Another approach involves strengthening the connection with one's future self, for example by writing a letter to oneself in ten years' time, so that long-term consequences feel more real.

None of this means that practical tools are useless. But recognising the emotional roots of procrastination may explain why so many people who own expensive planners still find themselves cleaning the kitchen at midnight instead of working.

texts.title: The paradox of choice reconsidered
q: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN: The original jam study found that more people bought jam when fewer varieties were offered.
TRUE
TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN: The meta-analysis concluded that choice overload never occurs.
FALSE (it found the average effect was close to zero, but the effect appeared under certain conditions).
List two conditions under which choice overload seems more likely.
When options are hard to compare, when people have no clear preferences, or when the decision is complex or time-limited.
What does the writer suggest about the way findings spread?
Simple, surprising findings can spread widely before they have been properly replicated.
paras: Few findings in behavioural science have enjoyed the popular success of the "paradox of choice". The idea, popularised in the early 2000s, holds that beyond a certain point additional options do not liberate us but paralyse us, leaving us less likely to decide at all and less satisfied when we do. Its emblematic study is now famous: shoppers presented with twenty-four varieties of jam at a tasting stand were far more likely to stop and look than those offered six, yet considerably less likely to buy.

The appeal of the finding is not hard to understand. It flatters a widespread intuition that modern life is overwhelming, and it carries a counter-intuitive twist that lends itself to talks and magazine articles. Businesses seized on it as a rationale for trimming product ranges; policy makers invoked it when designing pension schemes.

Yet the evidence has proved considerably less robust than its fame would suggest. Attempts to replicate the jam study produced mixed results, and a meta-analysis pooling data from dozens of experiments found that the average effect of large assortments on choice was, in effect, indistinguishable from zero. Taken at face value, this would seem to consign the paradox to the growing pile of psychological findings that have not survived closer scrutiny.

The picture, however, is more nuanced. A later analysis argued that the near-zero average concealed considerable variation: choice overload did emerge reliably, but only under particular conditions. It was more likely when the options were difficult to compare, when people lacked clear prior preferences, when the decision itself was complex, and when they were under time pressure. Where these conditions were absent, larger assortments were often welcomed.

The episode is instructive less for what it reveals about jam than for what it reveals about how findings travel. A simple, surprising result can acquire the status of received wisdom long before the slower, less exciting work of replication has been done, and by the time the qualifications arrive, few people are still listening.

texts.title: Booking a language course (phone call)
q: What is the caller's surname?
Haddad (H-A-D-D-A-D)
How many hours a week is the intensive course?
15 hours
What day does the evening course start?
Monday the 3rd
How much is the deposit?
Where should the caller go on the first day?
Room 12 on the second floor (reception first)
paras: RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Westbridge Language Centre. How can I help you?
CALLER: Hi, I'd like some information about your English courses, please. I'm thinking of joining one next month.
RECEPTIONIST: Of course. Are you interested in a general course or exam preparation?
CALLER: Exam preparation, I think. I need IELTS for a university application.
RECEPTIONIST: Right. We have two options. There's the intensive course, which is fifteen hours a week, mornings only, and there's an evening course, which is six hours a week over two evenings.
CALLER: I work during the day, so the evening one would be better.
RECEPTIONIST: No problem. The next evening course starts on Monday the third and runs for ten weeks. Classes are on Mondays and Wednesdays from six thirty to nine thirty.
CALLER: And how much does it cost?
RECEPTIONIST: It's four hundred and twenty pounds for the full course, and that includes all the materials and two practice tests. To reserve a place, we ask for a deposit of eighty pounds.
CALLER: Okay, that sounds fine. Can I book now?
RECEPTIONIST: Certainly. Can I take your name?
CALLER: Yes, it's Karim Haddad.
RECEPTIONIST: Could you spell your surname for me?
CALLER: H-A-D-D-A-D.
RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. And a contact number?
CALLER: Zero seven seven double four, five two nine, eight one six.
RECEPTIONIST: Great. On your first evening, please come to reception ten minutes early so we can give you your student card. After that, your class will be in Room twelve, on the second floor.
CALLER: Room twelve, second floor. Perfect. Thanks very much for your help.
RECEPTIONIST: You're welcome. See you on the third.

texts.title: A talk on urban heat islands
q: How much warmer can city centres be than the surrounding countryside at night?
Up to 7 degrees Celsius
Name two causes of the urban heat island effect mentioned.
Dark surfaces absorbing heat; lack of vegetation; heat from vehicles and air conditioning; buildings trapping heat.
What happened to roof temperatures in the white-roof project?
They fell by around 20 degrees on hot afternoons.
Why does the speaker say trees are better than white roofs?
They cool the street level where people actually are, and provide shade and other benefits.
paras: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that affects more than half of the world's population, often without them realising it: the urban heat island effect.

Put simply, cities tend to be warmer than the countryside around them. During the day the difference may be modest, but at night it can be dramatic. On calm, clear nights, the centre of a large city can be as much as seven degrees warmer than nearby rural areas.

So why does this happen? There are several reasons. First, the materials we build with, such as asphalt, concrete and dark roofing, absorb a great deal of the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly after dark. Second, cities have far less vegetation. Plants cool their surroundings by releasing water through their leaves, a process called evapotranspiration, so replacing fields and trees with buildings removes a natural cooling system. Third, cities generate heat of their own, from vehicles, industry and, ironically, air conditioning units. And finally, tall buildings close together trap warm air and reduce wind.
This matters because heat is not just uncomfortable; it is dangerous. During heatwaves, death rates rise significantly, particularly among elderly people and those living in poorly ventilated flats.

What can be done? One widely publicised approach is painting roofs white. In one project I was involved with, roof surface temperatures fell by around twenty degrees on hot afternoons. That's impressive, but there's a catch: the cooling mostly benefits the top floor, not the street below, where people actually walk and wait for buses.

That's why many researchers, including me, believe trees are a better long-term investment. They cool the air at street level, provide shade, absorb rainwater and improve people's mental well-being. The challenge, of course, is that trees take years to grow, which is why cities need to start planting now.

texts.title: Seminar: does social media polarise us?
q: What is the "filter bubble" hypothesis?
That algorithms show people only content that confirms their existing views, isolating them from opposing opinions.
What did the deactivation experiment find about polarisation?
Leaving the platform reduced polarisation only slightly, and on some measures not at all.
According to Dr Mensah, what may matter more than exposure?
How opposing views are encountered: often in their most hostile, mocking form.
What does the student suggest at the end?
That the platforms' incentives for engagement, rather than the algorithms alone, are the real problem.
paras: TUTOR: Right, let's pick up from last week. The question on the table is whether social media is actually driving political polarisation, or whether we're simply blaming it for trends that were already under way. Amira, you were going to start us off.

AMIRA: Yes. So the popular argument is the "filter bubble" hypothesis: algorithms learn what we like and feed us more of it, so we end up sealed off from anyone who disagrees. It's intuitively appealing, but the evidence is surprisingly thin. Several large studies have found that most users actually encounter a fair amount of content from the other side.
TUTOR: So the bubbles are leakier than we assumed.

AMIRA: Exactly. And there was an experiment where thousands of people were paid to deactivate their accounts for a month before an election. They were happier on average, and slightly less informed, but the effect on polarisation was modest at best, and on some measures negligible.
TUTOR: Dr Mensah, you've worked on this. Does that square with your findings?

MENSAH: Broadly, yes, but I'd add a caveat. The question isn't only whether people see opposing views, but in what form they see them. On most platforms, the content about the other side that travels furthest tends to be the most outrageous: the angriest post, the most ridiculous quote, often shared in order to mock it. So you're exposed to the other side, but to a caricature of it.
AMIRA: Which might actually make things worse than not seeing it at all.
MENSAH: Potentially, yes. Exposure isn't automatically a cure.
TUTOR: Leon, you look unconvinced.

LEON: Not unconvinced, just... I think focusing on algorithms lets the companies off the hook. The algorithm is only doing what it's been told to do, which is maximise engagement. If outrage keeps people scrolling, outrage gets promoted. Surely the problem is the business model, not the code.
TUTOR: That's a nice place to leave it. For next week, I'd like you each to find one study that challenges your own position.

texts.title: The benefits and limits of remote work
paras: Since 2020, remote work has shifted from an occasional arrangement to a normal part of working life for millions of employees. This essay examines the main advantages and disadvantages of working from home and argues that a hybrid model is likely to offer the most balanced solution.

The most obvious benefit of remote work is the time saved by not commuting. In large cities, employees may spend more than an hour travelling each day, and eliminating this journey can improve both well-being and productivity. In addition, working from home allows people greater flexibility to organise their day, which can be particularly valuable for parents and carers. From an employer's point of view, reduced demand for office space can lead to significant savings.

However, remote work also has clear drawbacks. Many employees report feeling isolated, and the boundary between work and private life can become blurred, with some people finding it difficult to switch off at the end of the day. Furthermore, there is evidence that younger staff in particular may lose out, since they learn a great deal by observing more experienced colleagues, something that is much harder to do through a screen. Collaboration and creativity may also suffer when spontaneous conversations no longer take place.

Taking these factors into account, a hybrid approach, in which employees spend part of the week in the office and part at home, appears to combine the strengths of both models. Office days can be reserved for meetings, training and teamwork, while home days can be used for tasks that require concentration.

In conclusion, remote work is neither a perfect solution nor a passing trend. Organisations that design flexible arrangements carefully, paying attention to the needs of different groups of employees, are likely to benefit the most.

texts.title: Should university education be free?
paras: Few questions in education policy provoke as much debate as whether higher education should be funded by the state or by students themselves. While there are compelling arguments on both sides, this essay contends that free tuition, if poorly targeted, may do less to promote fairness than its supporters claim.

Advocates of free university education typically argue that it removes a significant financial barrier to participation, particularly for students from low-income families. A degree is widely regarded as a public good: graduates tend to earn more, pay more in tax and contribute to innovation and civic life. From this perspective, it seems reasonable that society as a whole should bear the cost. Moreover, the prospect of substantial debt may deter talented students from applying at all, which represents a loss not only for the individuals concerned but for the economy.

Nevertheless, the case is less straightforward than it first appears. In most countries, students from wealthier backgrounds remain considerably more likely to attend university. Consequently, a policy of universal free tuition can, in effect, transfer resources from taxpayers in general, many of whom never attended university, to a relatively privileged group. Furthermore, evidence from several countries suggests that the main obstacles facing disadvantaged students arise long before the age of eighteen, in the form of unequal schooling and limited guidance, rather than at the point of application.

It could therefore be argued that the most effective use of public money lies elsewhere: in generous maintenance grants for low-income students, who often struggle more with living costs than with fees, and in investment in early education. Income-contingent loan systems, in which repayments depend on future earnings, may also offer a fairer compromise than either full fees or none.

In conclusion, the goal of widening access to higher education is widely shared, but free tuition is a blunt instrument for achieving it. Targeted support is likely to deliver greater fairness at a lower cost.

texts.title: Language, thought and the limits of linguistic relativity
paras: The proposition that the language we speak shapes the way we think has enjoyed a curious intellectual career. Associated, somewhat loosely, with the work of Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, it was enthusiastically embraced in the mid-twentieth century, largely discredited in the decades that followed, and has since been rehabilitated in a considerably more modest form. This essay argues that the contemporary evidence supports a weak version of linguistic relativity while giving little comfort to the strong, deterministic claims with which the hypothesis is often, and unfairly, conflated.

The strong version, which holds that language determines the categories available to thought, has fared poorly. Speakers plainly can entertain concepts for which their language lacks a dedicated word, and translation, however imperfect, would scarcely be possible were each language a sealed conceptual system. Moreover, several celebrated examples cited in support of the hypothesis, such as the supposedly vast vocabulary for snow in Inuit languages, have turned out to rest on misunderstandings of how those languages form words.

The weaker claim, namely that linguistic habits influence attention, memory and categorisation at the margins, is a different matter. Experimental work on colour perception, for instance, has shown that speakers of languages which have separate words for two shades of blue discriminate between those shades slightly faster than speakers of languages which do not. Similarly, communities whose languages describe spatial relations in absolute terms ("to the north of") rather than relative ones ("to the left of") appear to remember the arrangement of objects differently. Such effects are measurable and can be repeated; they are also, crucially, small, and frequently diminish when speakers are distracted from verbalising the task.

What emerges, then, is a picture of language not as a prison but as something closer to a set of well-worn paths: routes that thought travels easily and habitually, without being confined to them. This more temperate formulation lacks the rhetorical appeal of its predecessor, yet it has the considerable advantage of being consistent with the evidence.

texts.title: Unit 1 · What really makes us human?
q: Which ability does the writer think is most unusual in humans?
Imagining and planning for situations that have not happened yet.
Why does the writer mention crows and chimpanzees?
To show that tool use and problem-solving are not unique to humans.
paras: For centuries, people have tried to identify a single feature that separates humans from every other species. Tool use was once a popular answer, until researchers watched crows bend wire into hooks and chimpanzees use sticks to fish for insects. Language seemed a safer choice, yet many animals communicate in surprisingly complex ways.

Perhaps the most convincing candidate is our ability to imagine. We can picture events that have never happened, plan for a future we cannot see and feel nervous about a job interview that is still a week away. We also tell stories about ourselves, and these stories change as we move through life: the toddler having a tantrum becomes the teenager who is sure that nobody understands them, then the adult who settles down, gets promoted and eventually looks back with a mixture of pride and regret.

Another distinctive trait is how much we care about what others think. We blush, we apologise and we feel embarrassed on behalf of strangers. None of these characteristics makes us better than other animals, but together they explain why human life is so full of plans, worries and second thoughts.

texts.title: Unit 2 · A man of few words
q: Why did the writer stop using long words?
Because readers found them tiring and the message got lost.
What does "to eat your words" mean in the last paragraph?
To admit that something you said was wrong.
paras: When I started writing for a living, I thought impressive vocabulary was the key to good writing. I would never say "use" if I could say "utilise", and I filled every paragraph with adverbs: extremely, incredibly, absolutely. My editor, a man of few words, read my first article, crossed out half of it and wrote one comment in the margin: "Shorter."

I was annoyed at first. I went over the piece again and again, convinced that he had misunderstood it. But slowly I realised he was right. Readers do not want to fight their way through a sentence; they want to understand it quickly. Long words often hide a lack of clear thinking, and too many adverbs make every statement sound equally dramatic, which means none of them is.

These days I jot down my ideas in plain language first and only look for a better word when the plain one is genuinely not good enough. I still love language, but I love it most when it is precise. And yes, I had to eat my words: the editor and I are now good friends, and he still cuts my articles in half.

texts.title: Unit 3 · Enough is enough?
q: What happened to the town's population between 2010 and 2020?
It rose sharply, by about 40 per cent.
What is the main argument of the people who want to limit growth?
That roads, schools and water supplies cannot keep up.
paras: Ten years ago, Westford was a quiet market town of 20,000 people. Then a new railway line opened, cutting the journey to the capital to forty minutes, and the town began to change. By 2020 the population had risen sharply, by around 40 per cent, and house prices had more than doubled.

Not everyone is happy about it. Local residents complain that roads are permanently congested, that schools are full and that the town's water supply is struggling to keep up. A campaign group is now calling on the council to stop approving new housing developments until the infrastructure has caught up. "Growth is not automatically a good thing," says one of its organisers. "At some point you have to ask whether more is actually better."

Supporters of growth disagree. They point out that the new residents have brought money into the town, that unemployment has fallen steadily and that several shops which were about to close are now doing well. Slowing things down, they argue, would simply push prices up even further and keep young local people out of the market.
The council is expected to make a decision next month, and whichever way it goes, someone is going to be disappointed.

texts.title: Unit 4 · Can we trust our memory?
q: What did the experiment show about the word used in the question?
When the word "smashed" was used, people remembered higher speeds and even broken glass that wasn't there.
What does the writer recommend police do?
Record a witness's first account as early as possible and avoid leading questions.
paras: Most of us assume that memory works like a video camera, recording events so that we can play them back later. In reality, it is much less reliable. Every time we remember something, we rebuild it, and small details can change without our noticing.

In a famous series of experiments, people watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they "hit" each other. Others were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other. The second group estimated higher speeds, and a week later some of them even remembered seeing broken glass that had never been in the film.

This has serious consequences for the courts. A witness may be completely sincere and still be wrong. They might have seen the face of a stranger in a newspaper, or they may have been influenced by the way a police officer asked a question. That doesn't mean witnesses must be lying; it means their memories can't be treated as proof.

For this reason, experts recommend that police record a witness's first account as early as possible and avoid questions that suggest an answer. It might seem a small change, but it could prevent innocent people from going to prison.

texts.title: Unit 5 · Culture shock in both directions
q: What surprised the visitors most about British cities?
How little people spoke to strangers, even when they were sitting close together.
What does the writer say about stereotypes?
They contain a small amount of truth but hide how different individuals are.
paras: When we talk about culture shock, we usually think of people from rich countries travelling somewhere unfamiliar. But the experience works in both directions. A group of village elders who visited Britain for the first time were asked what had surprised them most. It wasn't the traffic or the tall buildings. It was how little people spoke to each other.

"On the train, everyone sat close together, but no one said a word," one of them explained. "At home, if you sit next to someone, you ask about their family." They were also puzzled by the number of old people living alone, and by the idea that you might have to make an appointment to visit a friend.

Of course, the British visitors who later stayed in their village had their own surprises. They found it hard to get used to having no privacy, and they were not sure how to respond when strangers asked how much they earned.

Stereotypes about nationalities usually contain a small amount of truth, but they hide how different individuals are. The British are said to be reserved, yet anyone who has been to a football match knows that isn't always the case. Getting to know people one by one is the only real cure for culture shock.

texts.title: Unit 6 · Good things that came from bad times
q: Name two inventions or changes that the text links to the First World War.
Wristwatches, blood banks, plastic surgery, women entering new jobs (any two).
Does the writer think war is worth these benefits?
No: the writer says these benefits came at a terrible price.
paras: It is difficult to think of anything positive coming out of the First World War, a conflict in which millions of people lost their lives. Yet historians point out that several features of modern life can be traced back to those years.

Wristwatches, for example, became popular because soldiers needed to check the time without taking a watch out of their pocket. Doctors developed new ways of storing blood, which led to the first blood banks, and surgeons who treated terrible facial injuries laid the foundations of modern plastic surgery. At home, women took over jobs that had always been done by men, and in many countries this helped to strengthen the case for giving women the vote.

What is important to remember, however, is that none of these changes needed a war to happen. Never should we pretend that progress justifies the suffering that produced it. It was the price that was paid, not the benefits, that the survivors remembered for the rest of their lives.
Studying this period does teach us something, though: people are remarkably inventive under pressure, and even in the worst circumstances they do find ways to help one another.

texts.title: Unit 7 · Seven small habits of happier people
q: Why does the writer say "if I were you" advice often fails?
Because people give advice for their own lives, not yours.
Which habit involves other people?
Doing small kind things for others / staying in touch with friends.
paras: Happiness research has become a big industry, and a lot of it is common sense dressed up in scientific language. Still, some findings are worth repeating, because most of us don't act on them.

First, people who spend money on experiences tend to feel better than those who spend it on things. A concert stays with you; a new phone becomes normal within a week. Second, small acts of kindness make the giver happier as well as the receiver. Third, staying in touch with friends matters more than almost anything else. If you had asked me ten years ago, I would have said that success at work was the key. If I had listened to the research, I would be less stressed now.

Fourth, sleep and exercise are not optional extras. Fifth, comparing yourself with others on social media rarely ends well. Sixth, writing down a few things you are grateful for each evening seems to work for many people. And finally, be careful with advice. When someone says, "I wouldn't do that if I were you," remember that they are imagining their own life, not yours. As if anyone could tell you exactly how to be happy!

texts.title: Unit 8 · Who stays at home?
q: What change does the text describe?
More fathers are staying at home to look after children while their partners are the main earners.
What problem do stay-at-home fathers mention?
Feeling isolated, for example at baby groups mostly attended by mothers.
paras: In many countries, the number of fathers who stay at home to look after their children has grown steadily over the past twenty years. In most of these families, the mother, whose salary is often higher, has become the main breadwinner, while the father takes responsibility for the domestic side of life.

Fathers who have made this choice describe it as rewarding but sometimes lonely. One man, who gave up a job in sales to care for his twin daughters, said that the hardest part was not the cooking or the cleaning. "It was walking into a baby group full of mothers and feeling that everyone was looking at me," he explained. "They were just being friendly, but I felt like an outsider."

Attitudes are changing, however. Employers are offering longer paternity leave, and children who grow up seeing both parents doing housework are less likely to see it as women's work. Some experts warn that the change is slower than headlines suggest: in most homes, women still do the majority of unpaid work, including the invisible task of organising everything.
Just how equal things will become remains to be seen, but the idea that caring is a job only for women is clearly losing ground.

texts.title: Unit 9 · Why music moves us
q: According to the text, why do songs bring back memories so strongly?
Music is linked to emotion, and emotional moments are remembered more strongly.
What does "mind you" introduce in the last paragraph?
A point that limits or contrasts with what was said before.
paras: Quite honestly, it is hard to explain why a few notes can make us cry. Music has no obvious practical use: you can't eat it, and it won't keep you warm. Yet every human culture we know of has created it, which suggests that it plays an important role in our lives.

One explanation is that music is closely linked to emotion. Hearing a favourite song releases chemicals in the brain associated with pleasure, the same ones involved in eating good food. Because emotional moments are remembered more strongly than ordinary ones, songs we heard at important times in our lives can bring back memories with surprising force. Unfortunately, this works both ways: a song from a painful period can be almost impossible to listen to.

Music also brings people together. Singing in a choir or dancing at a wedding creates a feeling of belonging that is difficult to achieve in other ways. After all, it is hard to stay angry with someone you have just sung with.

Mind you, not everyone responds to music in the same way. A small number of people feel nothing at all when they hear it, which reminds us that even the most universal experiences are not quite universal.

texts.title: Unit 10 · The power of believing
q: What is a placebo?
A treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill.
What surprising result does the text mention about telling patients?
Placebos seemed to work even when patients were told they were taking a placebo.
paras: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill or a salt-water injection. It is said to be one of the most powerful tools in medicine, and it appears to work for a surprising range of conditions, especially pain, nausea and anxiety.

In drug trials, patients are usually divided into two groups: one receives the real medicine and the other a placebo. A new drug is only considered effective if it performs better than the placebo, and this is often harder than it sounds. In some studies, around a third of the placebo group were reported to feel significantly better.

Even more surprisingly, placebos seem to work in some cases when patients are told exactly what they are taking. Researchers believe that the ritual of treatment itself, seeing a doctor, being listened to and taking something regularly, may trigger the body's own pain-relieving chemicals.

This does not mean that the effect is "all in the mind", or that serious illnesses can be cured by positive thinking. It is thought to have clear limits. What it does suggest is that the relationship between mind and body is far closer than we tend to assume.

texts.title: Unit 11 · Too clever for its own good
q: What does the writer mean by "feature creep"?
Adding more and more functions to a product until it becomes hard to use.
What prediction does the writer make?
That simple, reliable products will become a selling point again.
paras: My new washing machine has twenty-four programmes, a touch screen and an app that will tell me on my phone when the washing has finished. I use exactly two of the programmes. The rest are, I suspect, there because the manufacturer needed something to put in the advertisement.

This is what designers call feature creep: a product gets more and more functions until it becomes harder to use than the simple version it replaced. Many household appliances now come with instructions longer than a short novel, and when something goes wrong, it is often the electronics rather than the motor that fails.

Manufacturers argue that consumers want choice and that connected devices will save energy, since a machine that knows the price of electricity can run when it is cheapest. That may be true. But I can't help thinking that by the time I have learnt how to use all these features, the machine will have been replaced by a newer model.
My prediction is that within ten years, simplicity will be a selling point again. A fridge that just keeps food cold and lasts twenty years might turn out to be the most advanced product of all.

texts.title: Unit 12 · The day everything changed
q: Why did the writer start running?
A doctor warned her about her health after a check-up.
What happened during the marathon?
She collapsed with heatstroke a few kilometres from the finish and was taken to hospital.
paras: I had never run further than the bus stop when my doctor told me, after a routine check-up, that I needed to change my lifestyle. I was forty, overweight and stressed, and I decided, rather dramatically, that I would run a marathon within a year.

The training went surprisingly well. I followed a plan, increased the distance gradually and, furthermore, started to enjoy it. Meanwhile, I lost weight and slept better than I had for years. By race day I felt ready.

It was, however, one of the hottest days of the year. I ignored the advice to slow down, and a few kilometres from the finish I collapsed. I woke up in hospital with heatstroke, surrounded by worried doctors. I did wonder, lying there, whether the whole project had been a terrible mistake.

Nevertheless, that day turned out to be a turning point. It taught me that being stubborn and being determined are not the same thing, and that listening to your body is a strength, not a weakness. I ran my first marathon successfully the following spring, slowly and carefully, and I have never been so proud to finish in the bottom half.
